patterns.usage_note: The plainest, most neutral member: everyday Japanese, no literary flavor, and equally at home in speech and writing. It works for one-off past events and for habits (朝起きるとすぐに…ことにしている). Because it rides on the conditional と, though, it inherits と's one real restriction: the main clause states what simply happens or happened, so no commands, requests, invitations or 〜つもり/〜(よ)う plans (帰るとすぐに電話してください ✗ → 帰ったらすぐに…). Reach for it whenever none of the literary siblings' extra flavor is wanted.

examples.ruby: 電気[でんき]を消[け]すとすぐに子[こ]どもは寝[ね]てしまった。
examples.english: The kids fell asleep as soon as I turned off the light.

examples.ruby: 朝[あさ]起[お]きるとすぐにコーヒーを入[い]れることにしている。
examples.english: I make a point of brewing coffee right after I get up in the morning.

examples.ruby: 駅[えき]に着[つ]くとすぐに母[はは]から電話[でんわ]がかかってきた。
examples.english: The moment I got to the station, my mother called.

patterns.usage_note: Stresses genuine simultaneity rather than mere succession, and is the only member of the family that also takes a bare noun (卒業と同時に); outside of time it doubles as a neutral "and at the same time / while also" linker (難しいと同時に面白い).

examples.ruby: 会議[かいぎ]が始[はじ]まると同時[どうじ]に停電[ていでん]した。
examples.english: The power went out just as the meeting started.

examples.ruby: 電車[でんしゃ]が出発[しゅっぱつ]すると同時[どうじ]にスマホの充電[じゅうでん]が切[き]れた。
examples.english: My phone died at the exact moment the train pulled out.

examples.ruby: 目[め]を閉[と]じると同時[どうじ]に眠[ねむ]りに落[お]ちた。
examples.english: I fell asleep the instant I closed my eyes.

patterns.usage_note: The た is part of the pattern (だ途端 after ん-stem verbs: 転んだ途端), so it is past-only, and the main clause must be past too. What follows should be sudden, outside the subject's control, and often unwelcome — the speaker reports it as a surprise, so no commands, intentions or plans (and none of the family allows those anyway). Where や否や implies the subject had been poised and moved deliberately, た途端 implies nobody saw it coming; that is the line between them.

examples.ruby: 立[た]ち上[あ]がった途端[とたん]、ひどいめまいがした。
examples.english: The moment I stood up, a wave of dizziness hit me.

examples.ruby: ドアを開[あ]けた途端[とたん]に、猫[ねこ]が外[そと]へ飛[と]び出[だ]した。
examples.english: The instant I opened the door, the cat shot outside.

examples.ruby: 会場[かいじょう]に到着[とうちゃく]した途端[とたん]、雨[あめ]が降[ふ]り出[だ]した。
examples.english: No sooner had I reached the venue than it started to rain.

glosses: the moment one does X, Y undoes it
patterns.usage_note: The only member built for repetition: each time X is done it is immediately undone or repeated, so it cannot describe a one-off event, and it almost always carries the speaker's exasperation; dictionary form frames the habit, た-form each individual instance.

examples.ruby: 片付[かたづ]けるそばから子[こ]どもがおもちゃを散[ち]らかす。
examples.english: No sooner do I tidy up than the kids scatter their toys again.

examples.ruby: 注意[ちゅうい]したそばから、彼[かれ]はまた同[おな]じミスをする。
examples.english: No sooner do I warn him than he makes the very same mistake again.

examples.ruby: 稼[かせ]ぐそばから使[つか]ってしまうので、貯金[ちょきん]が全[まった]く増[ふ]えない。
examples.english: I spend it as fast as I earn it, so my savings never grow at all.

patterns.usage_note: Formal written narration of a single past event; unlike た途端 the second clause is typically a deliberate action by someone who had been poised for it, and 否や may simply be dropped to leave the stiffer literary 〜や Although the second clause is a deliberate act, it is still reported as a past fact — no commands, intentions or negatives.

examples.ruby: ベルが鳴[な]るや否[いな]や、生徒[せいと]たちは教室[きょうしつ]を飛[と]び出[だ]した。
examples.english: No sooner had the bell rung than the students bolted out of the classroom.

examples.ruby: 犯人[はんにん]は警官[けいかん]の姿[すがた]を見[み]るや否[いな]や逃[に]げ出[だ]した。
examples.english: The culprit took off the instant he spotted the police officer.

examples.ruby: 発表[はっぴょう]が終了[しゅうりょう]するや否[いな]や、質問[しつもん]の手[て]が次々[つぎつぎ]と挙[あ]がった。
examples.english: Hands shot up one after another the moment the presentation ended.

patterns.usage_note: Literary and narrow: both clauses must share one subject, that subject cannot be the speaker, and what follows has to strike the speaker as unexpected or out of character; past events only, so no commands, intentions or habitual readings.

examples.ruby: 彼[かれ]は部屋[へや]に入[はい]るなり、黙[だま]って窓[まど]を開[あ]け放[はな]った。
examples.english: The moment he entered the room, he threw the window wide open without a word.

examples.ruby: 弟[おとうと]は帰宅[きたく]するなり、鞄[かばん]を放[ほう]り出[だ]して寝[ね]てしまった。
examples.english: The moment my brother got home, he flung down his bag and fell asleep.

examples.ruby: その女性[じょせい]は私[わたし]の顔[かお]を見[み]るなり、大声[おおごえ]で泣[な]き出[だ]した。
examples.english: The woman burst into loud sobs the instant she saw my face.

patterns.usage_note: The bare literary 〜や — や否や is this form with 否や tacked on, not the other way round. Alive today essentially only in novels and news narration: same "in one sweep" force as や否や but terser and markedly stiffer, and you will not hear it in ordinary conversation. Same restrictions apply: a single past event, main clause reported as fact, no commands, intentions or negatives.

examples.ruby: 電話[でんわ]が鳴[な]るや、彼[かれ]は受話器[じゅわき]をひったくった。
examples.english: The instant the phone rang, he snatched up the receiver.

examples.ruby: 男[おとこ]は札束[さつたば]を見[み]るや、目[め]の色[いろ]を変[か]えた。
examples.english: The moment the man laid eyes on the wad of bills, his eyes lit up.

examples.ruby: 会見[かいけん]が終了[しゅうりょう]するや、記者[きしゃ]たちは一斉[いっせい]に駆[か]け出[だ]した。
examples.english: No sooner had the press conference ended than the reporters all rushed off at once.

patterns.usage_note: Vivid narration of a past scene in which the second action begins before the first has even finished, as if the subject had been waiting to pounce — more dramatic than や否や; the following clause must be a plain past statement, never a command, invitation, intention or negative.

examples.ruby: チャイムが鳴[な]るが早[はや]いか、子[こ]どもたちは校庭[こうてい]へ駆[か]け出[だ]した。
examples.english: The instant the chime sounded, the children tore off toward the schoolyard.

examples.ruby: 母[はは]は私[わたし]の姿[すがた]を見[み]つけるが早[はや]いか、駆[か]け寄[よ]ってきた。
examples.english: The moment my mother spotted me, she came running over.

examples.ruby: そのニュースが流[なが]れるが早[はや]いか、店[みせ]の前[まえ]には長[なが]い列[れつ]ができた。
examples.english: No sooner had the news broken than a long line formed in front of the shop.
